fullText: Paper and cardboard. Paper and cardboard are among the most widely recycled materials in the world. And unlike many other materials, they can often be turned into new paper products several times before their fibers become too short and weak to be reused. The recycling process begins when used paper is collected and separated from materials that cannot be processed. It is then mixed with water and broken down into a thick pulp. Contaminants such as staples, plastic pieces, and other unwanted materials are removed before the pulp is cleaned and processed into new paper. Cardboard follows a similar process, but its long, strong fibers make it particularly useful for producing new packaging. Recycled cardboard can become shipping boxes, cereal boxes, paper bags, tissue products, and packaging for household goods. However, not every paper product can be recycled indefinitely. Each time paper fibers are processed, they become shorter. After several cycles, they may no longer be strong enough to form quality paper, which is why manufacturers often add some fresh fiber to recycled paper products. There are also materials that can interfere with recycling. Greasy pizza boxes, for example, are often difficult to recycle when heavily contaminated with food or oil, while clean cardboard is generally much easier to process. Glass. Glass is one of the few materials that can be recycled again and again without losing its basic quality. Unlike paper fibers, which become shorter with repeated processing, glass can theoretically be melted and remade into new glass products repeatedly. Most recycled glass comes from everyday containers such as bottles and jars. After collection, the glass is sorted, cleaned, and crushed into small pieces called clet. The clet is then melted in a furnace and formed into new containers or other glass products. One important challenge is color. Clear, green, and brown glass are often separated because manufacturers need specific colors for different products. Mixing incompatible materials can also cause problems. Ceramics, stones, and heatresistant glass, for example, can remain solid during processing and damage equipment or create defects in new glass. Recycling glass also saves raw materials. Instead of producing every new bottle from materials such as sand, soda, ash, and limestone, manufacturers can replace part of those ingredients with recycled glass. Because cullet melts at a lower temperature than many raw materials, using it can also reduce the energy required during manufacturing. Recycled glass doesn't always return as another bottle. Depending on the type and quality, it can be used in new containers, fiberglass insulation, glass beads, construction materials, and decorative products. Plastics. Plastic is one of the most widely used materials on Earth. But recycling it is considerably more complicated than recycling glass or metal. The reason is that plastic isn't a single material. There are many different types, each with different chemical properties and recycling requirements. You may have noticed numbers such as 1 through 7 inside the recycling symbol on plastic packaging. These identify different resin types. For example, PET number one is commonly used for water and soft drink bottles, while HDPE number two is used for milk jugs, detergent bottles, and many household containers. After collection, plastics are sorted by type and color, cleaned, and shredded into small pieces called flakes. These flakes can be melted and formed into pellets which manufacturers use as raw material for new products. Recycled PET, for example, can become new bottles, polyester clothing, carpets, and packaging. But plastic cannot always be recycled indefinitely. Heat and mechanical processing can degrade some polymers, and mixed or contaminated plastics are particularly difficult to recover. Thin films, multi-layer food packaging, and heavily contaminated items are often much harder to recycle than clean, rigid containers. There's also a growing technology called chemical recycling, which can break certain plastics down into their chemical building blocks, so they can potentially be used to make new plastic. Unlike conventional mechanical recycling, this approach can handle some materials that are difficult to process mechanically, although it is still developing and can require significant energy. Aluminum. Aluminum is one of the most valuable materials in the recycling system because it can be recycled repeatedly without losing its fundamental properties. The metal in an old beverage can can eventually become part of another can, car component, or building product without needing to be replaced by newly mined aluminum. The recycling process is relatively straightforward. Used aluminum products are collected and separated from other materials, then shredded or crushed and heated in a furnace until the metal melts. Impurities and coatings are removed, and the molten aluminum is cast into large blocks called ingots or rolled into sheets that manufacturers can use to make new products. One of aluminum recycling's biggest advantages is energy savings. Producing aluminum from recycled metal requires only a fraction of the energy needed to extract and refine aluminum from boxite ore. This is why used aluminum cans are especially valuable to recycling systems. And the applications go far beyond cans. Recycled aluminum can be turned into car parts, bicycle frames, window frames, building materials, cookware, aircraft components, and new packaging. Aluminum is also particularly well suited to recycling because it doesn't degrade in the same way materials like paper or some plastics do. A can doesn't become a lower quality metal simply because it has been melted and formed again. So, when an aluminum can is recycled, you're not just keeping one piece of packaging out of a landfill. You're recovering a metal that can remain part of the manufacturing cycle for generations. Steel. Steel is one of the most recycled materials on the planet. And unlike many materials, it can be recycled repeatedly without losing its fundamental strength. Since steel is used in everything from buildings and vehicles to food cans and appliances, enormous amounts of it enter the recycling system every year. The process often begins with scrap steel collected from demolished buildings, old cars, appliances, machinery, and discarded products. Powerful magnets can separate steel from many other materials because steel contains iron and is magnetic. The recovered metal is then shredded or cut into smaller pieces before being melted in a furnace. Molten steel can be cast into new shapes or rolled into sheets and bars for manufacturing. Recycled steel can become new cars, construction beams, railway tracks, pipes, appliances, tools, and even new food cans. One interesting advantage of steel is that it doesn't need to be recycled into the same product. An old car can become construction steel, while a discarded steel beam could eventually become part of another vehicle or appliance. Steel recycling also reduces the need to extract and process new iron ore. This means less raw material has to be mined while the energy and resources already invested in producing the original steel can be put to use again. From the steel frame of a skyscraper to the can in your kitchen cupboard, this material can move through the recycling system repeatedly, making it one of the most important metals in the circular economy. Copper. Copper is one of the most valuable metals to recycle because it can be reused repeatedly without losing its essential properties. It is also highly conductive, which means recycled copper can perform just as well as newly mined copper in electrical applications. A huge amount of recyclable copper comes from electrical wiring, plumbing pipes, motors, generators, transformers, and electronic equipment. Unlike many household recyclables, copper is often recovered directly from old products because its high value makes collection economically worthwhile. During recycling, copper containing materials are sorted and processed to separate the copper from insulation, plastics, steel, and other components. The recovered copper is then melted and refined, producing metal that can be used to manufacture new products. This makes copper particularly important in the transition toward modern energy technologies. Recycled copper can find its way into new electrical cables, motors, power equipment, plumbing systems, and renewable energy infrastructure such as solar and wind installations. Copper recycling also has an important advantage over mining. The metal is already concentrated inside discarded products, so manufacturers can recover it without extracting and processing as much new ore. An old electrical cable, for example, doesn't have to become another cable. Its copper can be recovered and eventually become part of a motor, plumbing pipe, transformer, or electrical grid component. Because copper combines high economic value, excellent recyclability, and enormous demand from electrical and construction industries, recovering it from old products is one of the most useful forms of metal recycling. Textiles. Textiles are among the most difficult everyday materials to recycle because a single piece of clothing can contain several different fibers, dyes, coatings, and other components. Still, enormous amounts of clothing and fabric can be recovered instead of simply being thrown away. Textile recycling starts with sorting. Clothing is separated by material, color, and condition. Items that are still wearable are often reused or resold, while damaged textiles can be processed into fibers or other materials. Natural fabrics such as cotton, wool, and linen can be mechanically shredded back into fibers. These recovered fibers can then be spun into yarn or turned into products such as insulation, cleaning cloths, stuffing, and lower grade fabrics. Synthetic textiles such as polyester and nylon can also be processed, and some technologies can chemically break them down into their original building blocks to produce new fibers. However, recycling clothing isn't always straightforward. A shirt made from 60% cotton and 40% polyester, for example, is much harder to recycle than a garment made entirely from one fiber. Zippers, buttons, elastic, prints, and chemical finishes can create additional challenges. That's why reuse is often preferable to recycling when clothing is still in good condition. A jacket that can be worn again keeps all the energy and materials used to manufacture it in service without requiring another manufacturing process. When recycling is necessary, however, old textiles can become new clothing fibers, carpets, insulation, furniture stuffing, industrial rags, and other useful materials. So the next time an old shirt reaches the end of its life, it doesn't necessarily have to become waste. Its fibers can have another life in an entirely different product. Wood. Wood can have a surprisingly long life after its original use. And recycling it is often different from recycling materials like glass or aluminum. Instead of being melted down, discarded wood is usually reused, repaired, chipped, or processed into new wood-based products. The first step is usually sorting. Clean, untreated wood can be separated from painted, treated, or contaminated wood because chemicals, nails, coatings, and other materials can affect how it can be processed. Large pieces of usable wood from old buildings, furniture, pallets, and construction projects can sometimes be recovered and used again as lumber. Wood that is too damaged or small for direct reuse can be shredded into chips or fibers. These recovered materials can then become particle board, MDF, wood panels, animal bedding, landscaping mulch, and paper products. Some waste wood is also processed into wood pellets or other fuels. Although using wood as a fuel is generally considered energy recovery rather than material recycling. One interesting example is the humble wooden pallet. Instead of being discarded after a single use, damaged pallets can be repaired and returned to service, while unusable pieces can be ground down and incorporated into other wood products. However, not all wood should enter the same recycling stream. Pressuret treated lumber, painted wood, and wood contaminated with chemicals may require specialized handling because they can contain substances that shouldn't be released during processing. From an old wooden pallet becoming another pallet to construction scraps becoming particle board, recycling and reusing wood allows a material that took years or decades to grow to remain useful long after its first purpose has ended. Rubber and tires. Rubber products, especially vehicle tires, are some of the most challenging materials to recycle because tires are engineered to be extremely durable. A modern tire isn't made from rubber alone. It can contain synthetic and natural rubber, steel reinforcement, textile fibers, carbon black, and various chemical additives. When an old tire reaches a recycling facility, it is usually inspected first. Tires that are still in good condition may be retreaded, giving them a new tread surface and extending their useful life without manufacturing an entirely new tire. Tires that are no longer suitable for reuse can be mechanically processed. Large machines remove the steel and textile reinforcement and shred the remaining rubber into smaller pieces. The resulting crumb rubber can then be used in products such as playground surfaces, athletic tracks, rubber mats, flooring, and certain road surfaces. One particularly interesting application is rubberized asphalt, giving discarded tires a second life in transportation infrastructure, batteries. Batteries are highly recyclable, but they require specialized recycling because they contain a mixture of valuable materials and potentially hazardous chemicals. Batteries should not simply be placed in a regular household recycling bin unless the local recycling system specifically accepts them. Different batteries contain different materials. Lead acid batteries used in cars contain lead and sulfuric acid. While rechargeable lithium ion batteries found in phones, laptops, power tools, and electric vehicles contain materials such as lithium, nickel, cobalt, copper, and aluminum. The recycling process depends on the battery type. Facilities first collect and sort batteries before safely discharging or dismantling them. Rechargeable lithium ion batteries may then be shredded in controlled conditions, allowing materials such as steel, copper, aluminum, and a powdery mixture called black mass to be separated. Black mass contains valuable battery materials that can be further processed and recovered. Lead acid batteries have an especially wellestablished recycling system. Their lead can be recovered and used to manufacture new batteries, while other components such as plastic cases can also be processed for reuse. Organic waste. Organic waste is different from materials like glass, metal, or plastic because it comes from living organisms and can naturally break down. It includes things such as food scraps, fruit and vegetable peels, coffee grounds, garden waste, and leaves. Instead of sending this material to a landfill, organic waste can be processed through composting or anorobic digestion. During composting, microorganisms break down organic matter in the presence of oxygen, gradually turning it into a dark, nutrient-rich material called compost. This can then be added to soil to improve its structure and provide nutrients for plants. Anorobic digestion works differently. Organic waste is placed inside a sealed environment without oxygen where microorganisms break it down and produce bio gas. Biogas can be captured and used to generate electricity, produce heat, or be upgraded into a fuel similar to natural gas. The remaining material known as digestate can also be used as a soil amendment when properly processed. Keeping organic waste out of landfills also matters because buried food and other organic materials can decompose without enough oxygen and produce methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. So rather than thinking of food scraps and yard waste as something that has reached the end of its life, organic recycling turns them back into useful resources, fertile soil, nutrients, and even renewable energy. Construction materials. Construction and demolition waste is one of the largest waste streams in the world, but a significant portion of it can be recovered and used again. It comes from demolished buildings, road projects, renovations, and construction sites. Unlike household recycling, construction recycling usually involves recovering individual materials from a mixture of debris. Concrete, bricks, asphalt, wood, steel, and other materials are separated before being processed according to their properties. Concrete is one of the most common examples. Old concrete can be crushed into smaller pieces and used as recycled aggregate in new concrete, road foundations, drainage systems, and construction fill. Instead of quarrying as much new stone, builders can reuse material that has already been extracted and processed. Construction sites can also recover steel beams, bricks, timber, doors, windows, and other components for direct reuse. In some cases, reusing an entire building component is even more beneficial than processing it into raw material because it preserves the energy and work that went into manufacturing it originally. However, construction waste isn't automatically recyclable. Materials contaminated with asbestous, hazardous chemicals, lead-based paint, or other dangerous substances require specialized handling. Asphalt. Asphalt is one of the most successfully recycled construction materials in the world. Most of the asphalt used for roads is made from a mixture of mineral aggregates bound together with a sticky petroleum based material called bumen. When an old road is resurfaced or removed, much of that material can be recovered instead of being discarded. The recycling process often begins with milling. Specialized machines remove the worn upper layer of a road and grind it into pieces known as reclaimed asphalt pavement or RAP. The recovered material is then crushed, screened, and processed before being incorporated into new asphalt mixtures. One of the biggest advantages of asphalt recycling is that the old pavement can become part of new roads and highways. Contractors can mix reclaimed asphalt with fresh aggregate and binder or in some projects use high proportions of recycled material. Asphalt can also be recycled on site. Some road rehabilitation techniques. Heat or process the existing pavement and reuse it without completely removing the road. This can reduce the amount of material that needs to be transported away and the amount of new material brought in. The recycling process isn't limited to old road surfaces either. Asphalt removed from parking lots, airport runways, and other paved areas can also be recovered because asphalt can be processed and reused multiple times. An old road doesn't necessarily have to end its life as construction waste. The pavement being removed today can become part of the road carrying traffic tomorrow, making asphalt a particularly practical example of material recycling. Gypsum plaster board. Gypsum plaster board, also known as drywall or gypsum board, is a common construction material used for interior walls and ceilings. Its main ingredient is gypsum, a naturally occurring mineral that is made into a core and sandwiched between layers of paper. Plaster board can be recycled by separating the gypsum from its paper covering. At a recycling facility, clean plasterboard waste is broken down and processed to remove contaminants such as screws, insulation, wood, and other construction debris. The recovered gypsum can then be processed into a powder and used to manufacture new gypsum products. One of the most useful aspects of gypsum recycling is that the material can return to new plaster board and drywall products. Recovered gypsum can also be used in certain cement and agricultural applications where it can provide sulfur and calcium to improve soil conditions. However, contamination is a major challenge. Plaster board that has been mixed with paint, adhesives, asbestous containing materials, or large amounts of other construction waste may require specialized handling and cannot always be recycled through ordinary gypsum recycling systems.
fullTextVi: Giấy và bìa cứng. Giấy và bìa cứng là một trong những vật liệu được tái chế rộng rãi nhất trên thế giới. Và không giống như nhiều vật liệu khác, chúng thường có thể được chế biến thành các sản phẩm giấy mới nhiều lần trước khi sợi của chúng trở nên quá ngắn và yếu để có thể tái sử dụng. Quá trình tái chế bắt đầu khi giấy đã qua sử dụng được thu gom và tách khỏi các vật liệu không thể xử lý được. Sau đó nó được trộn với nước và nghiền thành bột dày. Các chất gây ô nhiễm như ghim, miếng nhựa và các vật liệu không mong muốn khác sẽ được loại bỏ trước bột giấy được làm sạch và chế biến thành giấy mới. Các tông cũng tuân theo quy trình tương tự, nhưng các sợi dài và chắc chắn khiến nó trở nên đặc biệt hữu ích để sản xuất bao bì mới. Các tông tái chế có thể trở thành hộp vận chuyển, hộp ngũ cốc, túi giấy, sản phẩm khăn giấy và bao bì đối với hàng gia dụng. Tuy nhiên, không phải sản phẩm giấy nào cũng có thể tái chế vô thời hạn. Mỗi lần sợi giấy được xử lý, chúng sẽ trở nên ngắn hơn. Sau vài chu kỳ, chúng có thể không còn đủ bền để tạo thành giấy chất lượng, đó là lý do tại sao các nhà sản xuất thường thêm một số sợi tươi vào các sản phẩm giấy tái chế. Ngoài ra còn có những vật liệu có thể cản trở việc tái chế. Ví dụ, những hộp bánh pizza dính dầu mỡ thường khó tái chế khi bị nhiễm bẩn nặng thực phẩm hoặc dầu, trong khi bìa cứng sạch thường dễ xử lý hơn nhiều. Thủy tinh. Thủy tinh là một trong số ít vật liệu có thể tái chế nhiều lần mà không làm mất đi chất lượng cơ bản của nó. Không giống như sợi giấy, sẽ trở nên ngắn hơn khi xử lý lặp đi lặp lại, về mặt lý thuyết, thủy tinh có thể bị nóng chảy và làm lại nhiều lần thành các sản phẩm thủy tinh mới. Hầu hết thủy tinh tái chế đều đến từ các vật dụng đựng hàng ngày như chai và lọ. Sau khi thu thập, thủy tinh được phân loại, làm sạch và nghiền thành từng mảnh nhỏ gọi là clet. Sau đó, clet được nấu chảy trong lò và tạo thành các thùng chứa mới hoặc sản phẩm thủy tinh khác. Một thách thức quan trọng là màu sắc. Kính trong, xanh lá cây và nâu thường được tách riêng vì nhà sản xuất cần màu sắc cụ thể cho sản phẩm khác nhau. Trộn các vật liệu không tương thích cũng có thể gây ra vấn đề. Ví dụ, gốm sứ, đá và thủy tinh chịu nhiệt có thể vẫn ở dạng rắn trong quá trình xử lý và hư hỏng thiết bị hoặc tạo ra các khuyết tật trên kính mới. Tái chế kính cũng tiết kiệm nguyên liệu. Thay vì sản xuất mọi chai mới từ các vật liệu như cát, soda, tro và đá vôi, nhà sản xuất có thể thay thế một phần nguyên liệu đó bằng thủy tinh tái chế. Vì cá vụn tan chảy ở nhiệt độ thấp hơn so với nhiều nguyên liệu thô nên sử dụng nó có thể cũng làm giảm năng lượng cần thiết trong quá trình sản xuất. Thủy tinh tái chế không phải lúc nào cũng trở lại như một chai khác. Tùy theo chủng loại và chất lượng có thể sử dụng trong các thùng chứa mới, sợi thủy tinh cách nhiệt, hạt thủy tinh, vật liệu xây dựng và sản phẩm trang trí. Nhựa. Nhựa là một trong những vật liệu được sử dụng rộng rãi nhất trên Trái đất. Nhưng việc tái chế nó phức tạp hơn nhiều so với việc tái chế thủy tinh hoặc kim loại. Lý do là nhựa không phải là một vật liệu duy nhất. Có nhiều loại khác nhau, mỗi loại có đặc tính hóa học và yêu cầu tái chế khác nhau. Bạn có thể đã nhận thấy các số từ 1 đến 7 bên trong biểu tượng tái chế trên bao bì nhựa. Chúng xác định các loại nhựa khác nhau. Ví dụ PET số một thường được sử dụng cho chai nước và nước ngọt, trong khi HDPE số 2 được dùng làm bình sữa, bình đựng chất tẩy rửa và nhiều vật dụng gia đình thùng chứa. Sau khi thu gom, nhựa được phân loại theo chủng loại, màu sắc, làm sạch và băm nhỏ mảnh gọi là vảy. Những mảnh này có thể được nấu chảy và tạo thành dạng viên mà các nhà sản xuất sử dụng làm nguyên liệu thô nguyên liệu cho sản phẩm mới. Ví dụ, PET tái chế có thể trở thành chai mới, quần áo polyester, thảm và bao bì. Nhưng nhựa không phải lúc nào cũng có thể được tái chế vô thời hạn. Quá trình xử lý nhiệt và cơ học có thể làm suy giảm một số polyme và nhựa hỗn hợp hoặc bị ô nhiễm đặc biệt khó phục hồi. Màng mỏng, bao bì thực phẩm nhiều lớp và các mặt hàng bị ô nhiễm nặng thường khó xử lý hơn nhiều tái chế hơn so với các thùng chứa sạch, cứng. Ngoài ra còn có một công nghệ đang phát triển được gọi là tái chế hóa học, có thể phá vỡ một số loại nhựa nhất định vào các khối xây dựng hóa học của chúng, vì vậy chúng có thể được sử dụng để tạo ra mới nhựa. Không giống như tái chế cơ học thông thường, phương pháp này có thể xử lý một số vật liệu khó xử lý một cách máy móc, mặc dù nó vẫn đang phát triển và có thể cần năng lượng đáng kể. Nhôm. Nhôm là một trong những vật liệu có giá trị nhất trong hệ thống tái chế vì nó có thể được tái chế nhiều lần mà không làm mất đi các đặc tính cơ bản của nó. Kim loại trong một lon đồ uống cũ cuối cùng có thể trở thành một phần của một lon khác, linh kiện ô tô hoặc sản phẩm xây dựng mà không cần phải thay thế bằng nhôm mới khai thác. Quá trình tái chế tương đối đơn giản. Các sản phẩm nhôm đã qua sử dụng được thu gom và tách ra khỏi các nguyên liệu khác sau đó được băm nhỏ hoặc nghiền nhỏ và nung trong lò cho đến khi kim loại tan chảy. Các tạp chất và lớp phủ được loại bỏ, nhôm nóng chảy được đúc thành khối lớn gọi là thỏi hoặc cán thành tấm mà nhà sản xuất có thể sử dụng để tạo ra sản phẩm mới. Một trong những lợi thế lớn nhất của việc tái chế nhôm là tiết kiệm năng lượng. Sản xuất nhôm từ kim loại tái chế chỉ cần một phần năng lượng cần thiết để tách và tinh luyện nhôm từ quặng boxit. Đây là lý do tại sao lon nhôm đã qua sử dụng đặc biệt có giá trị đối với các hệ thống tái chế. Và các ứng dụng vượt xa những chiếc lon. Nhôm tái chế có thể biến thành phụ tùng ô tô, khung xe đạp, khung cửa sổ, vật liệu xây dựng, dụng cụ nấu ăn, linh kiện máy bay và bao bì mới. Phần lớn nhựa đường dùng làm đường được làm từ hỗn hợp khoáng chất cốt liệu liên kết với nhau bằng vật liệu dính từ dầu mỏ gọi là bumen. Máy móc chuyên dụng loại bỏ lớp mặt trên bị mòn và mài thành các phần được gọi là mặt đường nhựa tái chế hoặc RAP. Một trong những lợi thế lớn nhất của việc tái chế nhựa đường là mặt đường cũ có thể trở thành một phần của những con đường và đường cao tốc mới.
